name: Pokéfinder
description: A Pokémon-themed web app I built to get properly comfortable with Nuxt and consuming third-party APIs. Pokémon is one of my favourite games, which made it an easy project to keep pushing on.

Built on Nuxt to learn its data fetching and rendering properly
Chosen as a subject I would actually keep working on

name: Sentrix
description: A storefront and staff back office for a security and surveillance retailer trading across eight branches. Stock, pricing and order visibility are all per branch, so opening a branch is a database insert rather than a deployment.
detail: Sentrix is a Laravel 13 API behind Sanctum with a Vue 3 single-page app on top, serving two audiences from the same data: customers browsing a branch's catalogue, and staff working orders, stock, vouchers and content from behind a permission wall. I built it to get properly comfortable with per-branch inventory and an authorisation model that actually holds up on the server rather than just hiding buttons.
features: Stock lives on a branch–product pivot, so availability, pricing and orders all follow the branch the customer picked
Checkout is a single transaction that locks the stock rows first, so a failure can never leave some lines decremented and others not
Seventeen permissions across seven staff roles — a branch manager can correct their own shelf count without seeing another branch's orders
Vouchers come in four types, are capped at the cart value, and record every redemption
Money is handled in centavos throughout and never touches a float
Staff dashboard with a paid-revenue chart and a searchable low-stock panel

name: My Notes
description: A pastel masonry notes board on the TALL stack, with live search and a confirm-then-undo-proof delete. Every note is a UUID row that only its owner's session can touch, enforced on the server rather than hidden in the UI.
detail: My Notes is a Laravel app built on the TALL stack — Tailwind, Alpine.js, Laravel and Livewire — using Volt single-file components so a page's markup and its class sit in one file instead of split across a controller and a Blade view. I built it to get past tutorial-level CRUD into the parts that actually matter: authorisation that holds even if a note's ID leaks, and a board that feels responsive without shipping a SPA framework for it.
features: Notes key on a UUID, not a sequential id, so a note's URL never hints at how many exist or whose turn is next
Every read, edit and delete re-checks a server-side policy — holding someone else's note UUID still gets you nothing
Search runs live against the title and body, debounced 300ms, with a skeleton shimmer while the round-trip is in flight
Each card takes a deterministic pastel hashed from its own UUID, so it keeps its colour across every re-render
Deleting asks for confirmation, animates the card out, then commits, with a toast on success
Livewire's wire:navigate moves between the board, the editor and the profile page without a full page reload

name: Forkcast
description: An AI calorie tracker built mobile-first: point a camera at a plate and a vision model names the foods and estimates portions, which land as calories and macros on the day's log. The scan sits behind an adapter with three providers, so the app runs with no API keys at all.
detail: Forkcast is a Next.js 16 App Router app on TypeScript and Tailwind v4, with Prisma 7 over Supabase Postgres and hand-rolled session auth rather than a drop-in provider. I built it to work through two things properly: a camera path that still works when the browser refuses getUserMedia, and an LLM dependency a reviewer can run without holding a key or paying for a single request.
features: The scan calls Anthropic when a key is set, OpenAI when only that one is, and a deterministic mock below that — so the app and its Playwright suite run at zero cost with no keys at all
Camera capture asks for the rear-facing stream and drops to a file picker when the browser refuses, with explicit denied and error states instead of a dead viewfinder
Onboarding computes targets from a Mifflin-St Jeor BMR, scales it by activity level, applies the goal delta, then splits 30/40/30 into protein, carbs and fat
Each log entry stores its own nutrition snapshot, so correcting a food later never rewrites what yesterday's total already said
A migration turns on row-level security across every table, so Supabase's anonymous PostgREST endpoint returns nothing while Prisma's role bypasses it
Insights is four Recharts cards — fourteen days of calories against target, the macro split, the weight trend, and a logging-streak heatmap
